content:
A Webb County sheriff's deputy turned off his body camera, told two women they had to "convince him" to let them go, and sexually assaulted one of them in his patrol car. On Oct. 6, U.S. District Judge Marina Garcia Marmolejo sentenced 29-year-old Ignacio Rodriguez IV to 20 years in federal prison.

The case, prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas and reported by Texas Border Business, is a stark accounting of what happens when the badge itself becomes the weapon.

What happened on Sept. 1, 2024

According to federal prosecutors, Rodriguez pulled over a car he said was driving into oncoming traffic on Sept. 1, 2024. He ordered the driver and her female passenger out of the car and told them to stand beside his marked patrol unit — then shut off his body-worn camera.

The passenger started recording on her own phone. What the recording captured, prosecutors said, was both women repeatedly asking to be let go while Rodriguez told them they needed to "convince him." He confiscated the driver's phone and ordered both women to follow his unit to a nearby desolate street.

Once there, Rodriguez ordered the driver into his patrol car — leaving the passenger behind — where he forced her to perform a sex act and groped her without consent, according to the prosecution's account. Rodriguez pleaded guilty on April 23 to deprivation of rights under color of law; a second count, for falsifying records in a federal investigation, was dropped under the plea deal.

How the system worked — and where it didn't

The sentence itself is a measure of accountability: 240 months in federal prison, five years of supervised release, sex-offender registration, no contact with the victims. The judge called his conduct "brazen, calculated, and extremely cruel." The FBI and the Laredo Police Department investigated; federal prosecutors took the case.

But the timeline deserves a look. According to the Laredo Morning Times, Rodriguez joined the Sheriff's Office as a correctional officer in 2021 and was promoted to deputy in November 2023. He resigned two days after the Sept. 2024 incident — before the criminal case even began. The guilty plea came in April 2026 and the sentencing in October 2026: more than two years from the assault to the sentence.

What Webb Watch is asking

What did the Sheriff's Office's own internal review find before Rodriguez resigned — and was anything referred for prosecution at the time? What changed, if anything, about body-camera policy and compliance audits after a deputy simply switched his off? And were there any other complaints on file against Rodriguez during his time in the agency? We will keep asking — because trust in a badge is rebuilt only when the institution that issued it answers for it.

Sources: Texas Border Business / U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of Texas, Oct. 6, 2026; Webb Watch 956 reporting.

excerpt: A former Webb County sheriff's deputy who shut off his body camera and sexually assaulted a woman during a 2024 traffic stop was sentenced to 20 years in federal prison. The badge didn't protect him — but how long did accountability take?
title: 20 Years for a Badge Turned Weapon: Former Webb County Deputy's Fall
